references.cite: Ling, S.J., Sanny, J., Moebs, W. (2016). University Physics Volume 2. OpenStax, Rice University. Free online textbook.
references.use: Beginner reading on work, heat and internal energy (work as the area under a pV curve, Sec. 3.2), the first law (Sec. 3.3), heat engines (Sec. 4.2) and the Carnot cycle (Sec. 4.5).

references.cite: Greitzer, E.M., Spakovszky, Z.S., Waitz, I.A. 16.Unified: Thermodynamics and Propulsion (lecture notes). Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
references.use: Free notes at the next step up from an intro physics book: Otto, Diesel and Brayton cycles (Ch. 3), entropy (Ch. 5) and the Brayton cycle on T-s coordinates (Ch. 6.4).

references.cite: NASA Glenn Research Center. Beginner's Guide to Propulsion: Turbine Engine Thermodynamic Cycle - Brayton Cycle.
references.use: Short illustrated explanation of the Brayton cycle stations and the T-s diagram.

references.cite: U.S. Department of Energy, Hydrocarbons and Geothermal Energy Office. How Gas Turbine Power Plants Work.
references.use: Plain-language description of compressor, combustor and turbine, and why higher firing temperature raises efficiency.

references.cite: U.S. Department of Energy, Alternative Fuels Data Center. How Do Diesel Vehicles Work?
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Basic Information about NO2.
references.use: What NOx is, where it comes from, and its health and environmental effects.

references.cite: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Basic Information about Carbon Monoxide (CO) Outdoor Air Pollution.
references.use: What CO is, its sources and health effects.

references.cite: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Particulate Matter (PM) Basics.
references.use: Definitions of PM10 and PM2.5 and why fine particles matter.

references.cite: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Sulfur Dioxide Basics.
references.use: Sources of SO2 (fuel sulfur) and its effects.

references.cite: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Understanding Global Warming Potentials.
references.use: Plain explanation of GWP and CO2 equivalent; lists the 100-year GWP of methane from the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report as 27-30.

references.cite: U.S. Energy Information Administration. Carbon Dioxide Emissions Coefficients.
references.use: CO2 per unit of heat for common fuels (natural gas vs distillate fuel oil), used to show that gas has less carbon per unit of energy.

references.cite: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Clean Air Technology Center (1999). Nitrogen Oxides (NOx), Why and How They Are Controlled. EPA-456/F-99-006R.
references.use: Overview of NOx formation and control techniques (combustion modification and post-combustion such as SCR) for a non-specialist reader.
